strengths: Novel and well-motivated methodological idea: decomposing the aggregate loss into per-datapoint and per-direction (Hessian eigenvector) components to reveal 'hidden' phase transitions obscured by scalar loss curves.

Strong theoretical grounding connecting the approach to existing literature on tiny training subspaces, linear mode connectivity, singular learning theory, and polygenic scaling effects, providing a coherent justification for why linear decomposition should be meaningful.

Clean and convincing synthetic validation on the arithmetic addition task, where POLCA clustering recovers both the digit-position skill and the more subtle 'carrying' skill (quantified via cluster homogeneity), while exact-loss clustering only recovers the former.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Appendix D, E, F) comparing POLCA against simpler decomposition strategies (Fisher information) and different basis choices (random orthonormal, shuffled Hessian), as well as validating the necessity of the second-order correction term.

Extension to a real natural language modeling task shows qualitatively interpretable clusters (e.g., appositive vs. non-appositive noun phrases, preposition prediction after a clause) that are plausible extensions of the synthetic setting's findings.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted only on very small models (9M and 40M parameters) with short training runs; it is unclear whether the identified 'hidden breakthroughs' and clustering results generalize to larger, more realistic LLMs, and the authors themselves flag Hessian-eigenvector computation as a serious scalability bottleneck.

The natural language modeling results, which are the paper's main claim to real-world relevance, are validated only qualitatively (a handful of contexts nearest the cluster medoid and automatic POS/token labeling), unlike the arithmetic setting where a quantitative homogeneity metric is used; this makes it hard to assess whether the reported clusters are representative or cherry-picked.

The basis ablation (Appendix E) shows that random orthonormal or randomly shuffled Hessian bases achieve carry-skill homogeneities (0.84-0.90) not too far below the full Hessian-eigenvector basis (0.90-0.97), which somewhat undercuts the paper's central methodological motivation for using expensive, iteratively-computed Hessian eigenvectors as an 'interpretable' basis.

The second-order approximation underlying POLCA relies on the assumption that basis vectors (aggregate Hessian eigenvectors) are also approximately eigenvectors of individual datapoint Hessians, which the authors explicitly acknowledge 'is unlikely to be correct'; the justification for proceeding despite this is only indirect (high average cosine similarity between first- and second-order estimates), not a rigorous error analysis.

Some example clusters reported (e.g., repeated <PAD> tokens, repeated newlines) appear to reflect superficial tokenization/formatting artifacts rather than genuine conceptual 'breakthroughs,' raising questions about how many of the discovered clusters are meaningful versus trivial.

The paper's central narrative claim -- that 'phase transitions are everywhere' and represent discrete, human-interpretable categorical concepts -- is asserted fairly strongly in the conclusion but is supported mainly by illustrative examples rather than systematic, large-scale quantitative evidence across many basis vectors/clusters.

Reproducibility could be a concern given the complexity of Algorithm 1 (iterative nullspace projection and eigenvector computation) and various under-specified hyperparameter choices (e.g., k, checkpoint intervals) that appear to be selected somewhat ad hoc for feasibility rather than principled reasons.

strengths: The core idea—disaggregating loss by data subset and decomposing it along Hessian-eigenvector directions to reveal 'hidden' phase transitions—is conceptually interesting and well-motivated by a coherent review of prior work on phase transitions, loss subspaces, and mode connectivity.

The POLCA extension of Loss Change Allocation (arbitrary orthonormal basis, per-example decomposition, second-order correction) is a reasonable technical contribution with a derivation provided in the appendix.

The synthetic arithmetic experiment provides a clean, controlled demonstration that POLCA clustering recovers the carry skill while exact-loss clustering fails, supported by a quantitative homogeneity metric.

Several useful ablations are included (decomposition strategy comparison, basis choice comparison, first- vs second-order approximation), which partially probe the sensitivity of the method to its design choices.
The natural language experiments show qualitatively plausible, human-interpretable clusters (e.g., appositive noun phrases, punctuation patterns) that are not visible in aggregate loss curves.
weaknesses: All experiments use very small models (9M and 40M parameter, 3-layer toy transformers) trained on limited data; there is no evidence the method scales to realistic LLM training, and the paper itself flags the Hessian-eigenvector basis computation as computationally prohibitive at scale without offering a validated cheaper alternative.

The natural language modeling results (Section 5), which are the paper's main claim to real-world relevance, are evaluated only qualitatively—via manual inspection of a handful of cluster examples and automatically-generated POS/token labels—with no quantitative cluster-quality or interpretability metric analogous to the carry-skill homogeneity used in the arithmetic setting.

The key approximation underlying POLCA's second-order term (Eq. 5–7) assumes that the aggregate Hessian's top eigenvectors are close to the datapoint-specific Hessian's top eigenvectors; the paper openly admits this assumption 'is unlikely to be correct' and offers only a weak empirical check (cosine similarity between first- and second-order terms) that does not actually validate the assumption itself.

There are no baselines from the broader interpretability/subspace literature beyond simple internal ablations (random orthonormal basis, shuffled Hessian, Fisher information), and these comparisons are only run in the synthetic setting, not in the more important NLM setting.
All results come from single training runs with no seeds/error bars, raising concerns about the robustness and statistical reliability of the discovered clusters and 'breakthroughs.'

The paper does not demonstrate any downstream utility of the discovered breakthroughs beyond post-hoc, subjective storytelling about what a cluster 'means'—there is a risk that HDBSCAN artifacts or arbitrary basis choices are being over-interpreted as genuine conceptual breakthroughs.

The method itself is an incremental combination of existing techniques (LCA, Hessian-eigenvector low-rank training subspaces, HDBSCAN clustering) rather than a substantially novel algorithmic contribution, and the paper's broader claims (e.g., 'phase transitions are everywhere,' discrete categorical learning) are speculative extrapolations not rigorously supported by the limited experiments shown.

Reproducibility is limited by the lack of code release mention and by compute-heavy design choices (per-checkpoint Hessian eigenvector computation) that are not clearly quantified in terms of wall-clock cost or feasibility for larger models.

strengths: The core idea—disaggregating loss by datapoint and decomposing it along Hessian-eigenvector directions to reveal 'hidden' phase transitions obscured by the aggregate loss curve—is conceptually novel and well-motivated by an extensive review of prior work on training dynamics, singular learning theory, and mode connectivity.

The method (POLCA) is a sensible and clearly derived extension of Loss Change Allocation (LCA), with a principled (if approximate) justification for including a second-order term when using Hessian-eigenvector bases.

The paper validates its claims in two settings (synthetic arithmetic addition and natural-language modeling on Wikipedia), and in both cases shows that POLCA clustering recovers concepts (e.g., 'carrying' in addition, appositive vs. non-appositive noun phrases) that are not recoverable by clustering on exact loss alone, which is a clean and interpretable demonstration of the central claim.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided: comparison against Fisher-information-based decomposition, random/shuffled bases vs. Hessian eigenvectors, and first- vs. second-order approximation error, which lend some support to the design choices.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful illustrative figures (e.g., Figure 1) that make the core intuition of 'hidden' breakthroughs accessible.
weaknesses: All experiments use very small models (9M and 40M parameters, 3 layers) trained for a single epoch/short run; there is no evidence or discussion of how well POLCA scales to realistic model sizes or longer training regimes beyond a brief remark in Limitations, which weakens the significance of the claims for the broader LLM community.

The quantitative evaluation is thin: the main numeric result is 'carry skill homogeneity' from a single synthetic run with no error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing; the natural-language evaluation is almost entirely qualitative/anecdotal (a handful of manually-inspected cluster examples and POS-tag labels), making it hard to assess the generality or reliability of the claimed interpretability gains.

The second-order approximation in POLCA relies on an assumption (that datapoint-level Hessian eigenvectors align with the aggregate top eigenvector direction) that the authors themselves say 'is unlikely to be correct' (Appendix A); while they show empirically that the first- and second-order terms are similar in this setting, this does not resolve the underlying theoretical inconsistency and its impact is only checked in the synthetic task.

There is no comparison against other established phase-transition/interpretability detection baselines beyond simple loss-curve clustering and per-token Fisher information; stronger baselines (e.g., other subspace decomposition or attribution methods) are not considered.

The practical cost of the method (iterative Hessian eigenvector computation via Lanczos at every checkpoint) is nontrivial, and while Appendix E suggests cheaper bases work almost as well, this is only validated on the small synthetic task, leaving open whether the approach is tractable at scale.

The interpretability claims for the natural-language clusters are somewhat subjective (manual labeling via top POS tags/tokens and 'closest contexts' inspection) without any human evaluation, inter-rater agreement, or quantitative interpretability metric, weakening confidence that the clusters robustly correspond to meaningful learned skills rather than superficial lexical patterns.

The paper's broader claims (e.g., 'phase transitions are everywhere', support for categorical/discrete learning of concepts) are somewhat overstated relative to the narrow empirical evidence, which is limited to two small-scale, short-duration training runs.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated extension of Loss Change Allocation (POLCA) that decomposes per-datapoint loss along an interpretable, iteratively-constructed Hessian eigenvector basis, combined with a principled second-order correction term.

Strong grounding in prior literature on low-rank training subspaces, singular learning theory, and phase transitions, giving a coherent theoretical justification for why linear decomposition should reveal hidden breakthroughs.

Thorough quantitative validation on the synthetic arithmetic task: cluster homogeneity, recall, and F1 scores clearly show POLCA recovers the 'carrying' skill that exact-loss and vanilla LCA clustering fail to find.

Extensive ablation studies (Appendices G, H, I) comparing POLCA against alternative decomposition strategies (Fisher information, LCA, first-order POLCA) and alternative bases (random orthonormal, shuffled Hessian), which strengthens the claim that both the basis choice and the second-order correction matter.

Natural language experiments show interpretable syntactic/lexical clusters (e.g., appositive vs. non-appositive noun phrases) with breakthroughs invisible in the aggregate/token loss curve, providing some external validity beyond the synthetic setting.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, dataset, setup) and clear, well-organized presentation of a fairly intricate mathematical method.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted only on very small models (9M and 40M parameters) and short training runs; the paper's own limitations section admits that Hessian-based basis computation and fine-grained checkpointing may not scale, leaving the practical applicability of the method to realistic LLM training largely unaddressed.

The key second-order approximation relies on the assumption that per-datapoint Hessian eigenvectors align with the aggregate Hessian eigenvector basis, which the authors themselves state is 'unlikely to be correct'; the empirical validation of this approximation is limited to a small sample (400 tokens, 10 checkpoints, 5 basis vectors) in only the synthetic setting.

The natural language evaluation is largely qualitative/anecdotal (a handful of selected clusters with manually refined labels) rather than a systematic quantitative evaluation comparable to the arithmetic setting; there is no ground-truth skill labeling or held-out validation of the recovered syntactic categories, and the automated POS-based labeling is acknowledged to miss many human-interpretable skills.
No comparison to other bottom-up/unsupervised interpretability baselines mentioned in the introduction (e.g., SAEs, PCA-based approaches) despite explicitly positioning the work relative to them.

The method involves many hyperparameters (basis checkpoint interval, k, POLCA checkpoint interval, HDBSCAN parameters, threshold τ for 'hidden' breakthroughs) whose sensitivity is not systematically explored beyond the specific configurations chosen for the two tasks used.

Computational cost (Hessian eigenvector estimation via Lanczos/Hessian-vector products at fine-grained checkpoint intervals) appears high, which combined with the small-scale-only experiments raises concerns about the broader significance/impact of the method for interpretability research on models of realistic size.

The paper's central claims about 'hidden breakthroughs' rely on a somewhat ad hoc operational definition (threshold τ, window Δ) that is not deeply justified or varied in sensitivity analysis, limiting confidence that the discovered transitions are robust rather than artifacts of the specific metric definition.

strengths: The core idea of decomposing aggregate loss into per-example, per-direction contributions to reveal 'hidden' phase transitions is a reasonable and underexplored extension of Loss Change Allocation (LCA) and low-rank training subspace literature.

The synthetic arithmetic-carrying experiment provides a clean, interpretable validation case with ground-truth skill labels, showing a scenario where exact-loss clustering demonstrably fails while the proposed POLCA decomposition succeeds.

Reasonably extensive ablations are provided in the appendix (basis choice: random orthonormal, shuffled Hessian, top eigenvectors; comparison to Fisher information and LCA; first- vs second-order approximation), which helps probe robustness of the method's design choices.

The natural language experiments produce clusters with plausible syntactic/lexical coherence (e.g., appositive phrases, tokens after commas), suggesting the method can surface some structure beyond what aggregate loss curves show.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted only on very small models (9M and 40M parameters) trained for very short schedules (10k–14k iterations) on small data samples, which is far removed from the scale at which the 'breakthroughs' the paper motivates (induction heads, grammar acquisition, hierarchical generalization) are actually studied in the literature; it's unclear the findings generalize beyond toy settings, and the paper's own limitations section admits scaling is a major open problem.

The core second-order justification is internally inconsistent: the paper argues at length that the second-order term is necessary because it 'could be expected to dominate,' yet Appendix I shows the first- and second-order approximations are nearly identical (L2 norm ~0.9999), undermining the stated motivation for the added complexity and calling into question the technical narrative.

The key approximation underlying POLCA's second-order term (that the aggregate Hessian eigenvector is close to the datapoint-specific Hessian eigenspace) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as 'unlikely to be correct,' yet is used anyway without rigorous quantification of its impact across settings (validation is limited to a small 400-token/5-basis-vector check in the arithmetic setting only, not in the language modeling setting where most of the paper's interpretability claims are made).

The 'hidden breakthrough' definition (Eq. 10) depends on an arbitrary threshold τ and window Δ with no sensitivity analysis showing that results are robust to these choices, undermining confidence in the quantitative claims (e.g., '0.355 fraction of clusters with hidden breakthroughs').

For the natural language setting, there is no ground-truth validation analogous to the arithmetic carry skill; interpretability claims rest on automatically generated POS-tag labels that are then manually 'refined' by the authors, introducing subjectivity with no inter-annotator agreement, blind evaluation, or automated interpretability scoring (e.g., LLM-judge based, as used in comparable SAE evaluation work the paper itself cites).

No demonstration of practical utility: despite motivating the method with potential applications to data curation, learning-rate scheduling, or critical-period-aware training, the paper provides no downstream experiment showing that identified 'breakthroughs' can inform or improve training decisions.

The method's computational cost (Hessian eigenvector estimation at many checkpoints) is substantial and explicitly flagged as a scalability bottleneck, limiting the significance of the contribution to small-scale, proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than a broadly applicable interpretability tool.

Baselines used for comparison (change in exact loss, Fisher information, vanilla LCA) are constructed by the authors and evaluated primarily via metrics the authors themselves define (homogeneity, hidden-breakthrough fraction), rather than against established/independent interpretability benchmarks, making it harder to assess how meaningful the reported improvements are.

The overall novelty is incremental relative to well-established prior work (LCA, Gur-Ari et al.'s low-rank training subspace, Michaud et al.'s quantization model of scaling), largely combining existing techniques rather than introducing a fundamentally new methodological insight.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated extension (POLCA) of Loss Change Allocation to arbitrary bases and per-example loss, with a clearly derived second-order correction and empirical validation of the approximation quality (Appendix C, I).

Strong grounding in prior literature on training dynamics, low-rank subspaces, and linear mode connectivity, giving a coherent theoretical justification for why linear decomposition should reveal interpretable directions.

The synthetic arithmetic experiment provides a clean, ground-truth validation: POLCA recovers the 'carrying' skill with high homogeneity (0.97) while exact-loss clustering and even LCA fail to do so, offering fairly convincing quantitative evidence for the core claim.

Extensive ablations are provided (decomposition strategy comparison, basis choice comparison, first- vs second-order approximation), which strengthens confidence that the specific design choices (Hessian-based basis, second-order term) matter.

Application to a real language model (Wikipedia LM) with automatic + manually verified POS-based labeling shows the method scales beyond toy settings and produces plausible, human-interpretable grammatical clusters.
Clear writing and useful visualizations (Figures 1, 3-5) that intuitively convey the core idea of aggregation obscuring sub-population phase transitions.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to very small models (9M and 40M parameters) trained on relatively short schedules; the paper's central motivating claim about breakthroughs in large language model training is never tested at a scale where this would matter most, and the authors themselves flag Hessian-eigenvector computation as a serious scalability bottleneck.

The natural language results (Section 5) are largely qualitative — no homogeneity/precision-style quantitative metric analogous to Table 1 is reported for the NL clusters, so the strength of the 'hidden breakthrough' claim there rests mainly on hand-picked examples and subjective cluster labels (e.g., 'repeated newline' clusters are arguably trivial/artifactual rather than conceptual breakthroughs).
The definition of 'hidden breakthrough' (Eq. 10) depends on an arbitrarily chosen threshold τ and window Δ, and no sensitivity analysis is provided to show the results are robust to these choices.

The second-order approximation relies on the assumption that datapoint-level Hessian eigenvectors align with the aggregate Hessian eigenvector b, which the authors explicitly acknowledge is 'unlikely to be correct'; while empirical RMSE is reported, this weakens confidence in the theoretical justification for using second order at all versus the cheaper first-order variant, which performs almost identically (Table 8, Appendix I).

Motivational claims in the introduction (e.g., informing data selection or learning-rate scheduling around breakthroughs) are never empirically tested; the paper stops at cluster discovery/interpretability without demonstrating any downstream utility.
No comparison against more established unsupervised interpretability baselines mentioned in the text (e.g., SAEs, PCA-based methods) despite explicitly positioning POLCA alongside them.
Results appear to be based on single training runs without seeds/variance reporting, raising questions about the robustness/reproducibility of the specific clusters and homogeneity numbers reported.
